chapter_theme: Gratitude: help is measured by its timing, its motive and the worth of the one who receives it, not by its size. Memory is ordered accordingly, so that good is kept and harm is let go, and ingratitude is called the one sin with no escape.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: help given without cause, in time or without calculation is immeasurable (101-103), any help grows with those who understand (104-105), do not abandon those who helped (106-107), forget harm (108-109), and the gravity of ingratitude (110).

101.reading: For help given when no help was given first, earth and heaven together are hardly repayment.
101.nuance: Parimelazhagar gives the reason: all repayment has a cause, and this help has none, so nothing can match it. He also records a variant reading, in which the helped person could not return it, which changes the focus from the giver's freedom to the receiver's helplessness.

positions.position: He reports another reading of the text, about help given to those unable to return it.
positions.quote: மறித்து உதவமாட்டாமை உள்ளவிடத்துச் செய்த உதவி என்று உரைப்பாரும் உளர்.

102.reading: Help given in its time, though small, is far greater than the earth.
102.nuance: Value here is relative to the need of the moment. Parimelazhagar's phrase is striking: it's the moment of mortal crisis that is being weighed, not the gift.

103.reading: If you weigh the good of help given by those who don't weigh the return, it is greater than the sea.
103.nuance: The verb தூக்கு is used twice: the giver doesn't weigh, and the recipient should. The three opening comparisons go from earth and heaven to earth to sea, and the verses seem interested in measure as such.

104.reading: Though the good done is only as much as a millet, those who understand its fruit take it as a palm.
104.nuance: The enlargement happens in the recipient's mind, and it isn't an error, it's a discipline. Parimelazhagar says the fruit in question is what comes to the one who regards it this way, so gratitude also benefits the grateful.

105.reading: Help is not bounded by the help given: its measure is the worth of those to whom it was done.
105.nuance: The verse repeats உதவி three times and it isn't clear which help is being measured.

positions.position: This concerns repayment: what the receiver gives back is measured by the receiver's own worth, not by the original help.
positions.quote: கைம்மாறான உதவி, காரணத்தானும் பொருளானும் காலத்தானும் ஆகிய மூவகையானும் முன் செய்த உதவியளவிற்று அன்று;

positions.position: This concerns the help itself: its value is judged by the quality of whoever receives it.

106.reading: Do not forget the bond of the stainless, and do not abandon the friendship of those who were your strength in sorrow.
106.nuance: Two different people are owed loyalty: those of good character and those who helped when it was needed. Parimelazhagar says the first serves the next life and the second this one. The second debt holds whatever the helper's character is.

107.reading: For all seven births they will remember the friendship of those who wiped away their sorrow.
107.nuance: துடைத்தவர், those who wiped, has a physical sense of wiping tears away. Parimelazhagar notes the past tense conveys speed, and he cites the lost Valaiyapathi for the phrase, which is a valuable thread.

positions.position: Seven births are meant literally: affection for the helper carries on in each birth.
Seven births is a figure of exaggeration meaning that there is no time limit.

108.reading: It's not good to forget a good done; what's good is to forget, that very day, what isn't good.
108.nuance: நன்று repeats through the verse, so 'good' is both the thing remembered and the act of letting go. Parimelazhagar says this is about one person who has done both good and harm, which is narrower than a general call to forget all wrongs.

109.reading: Even if they do something as painful as killing, it vanishes when one thinks of a single good they did.
109.nuance: This is a hard saying, as it places the burden on the injured person. Parimelazhagar explains it through 104: the millet taken as a palm outweighs everything. Kalaignar makes it more therapeutic, a way to keep from being wounded inside.

110.reading: Those who kill any good may have an escape, but there is no escape for one who kills a good done to him.
110.nuance: Ingratitude is ranked as the sin with no remedy. Parimelazhagar's list of lesser crimes comes from Purananuru 34, whose speaker makes the same comparison, so this verse is a direct thread to that poem.

positions.position: Even the great crimes, cutting a cow's udder, destroying a womb and killing a Brahmin, can be expiated, as Purananuru 34 lists.

links.note: Both use seven births. In 62 a child's character shields the parent, and in 107 memory of a helper persists. Parimelazhagar on 107 refers back to his explanation at 62, so he treats the phrase as one idea.

On Kalaignar's reading of 105, both make the recipient the measure of the gift: the guest's worth in 87 and the helped person's character in 105. Parimelazhagar's different reading of 105 separates them.

Help without weighing the return is vaster than the sea, and in 221 giving outside the destitute is a kind of expected repayment. The two define real generosity by lack of calculation, from the receiver's and the giver's sides.
The same millet and palm. Here others' small kindnesses are enlarged, and in 433 one's own small faults are. The same mental act, turned in opposite directions, gives gratitude and conscience.

source_issues: Parimelazhagar's comment on verse 107 refers to an explanation of the seven kinds of birth at verse 62, but his entry for 62 here is a duplicate of 61 (see ch007).
Parimelazhagar's comment on verse 110 is scrambled: its last sentences are out of order ('இதனால் செய்ந்நன்றி கோறலின் கொடுமை கூறப்பட்டது. முதலிய பாதகங்களைச் செய்தல்.').
Kalaignar's entry for verse 103 ends with a stray '104.'. Manakkudavar's entry for verse 107 ends with empty brackets.
